title: Business Logic and Use Cases
learning_outcomes: Explain how business logic and use cases affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from keeping business rules outside controllers to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on business logic and use cases in backend architecture for rest apis. You will connect keeping business rules outside controllers to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Business Logic and Use Cases matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying keeping business rules outside controllers deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Separate request transport, application use cases, domain rules, and persistence so each responsibility can be tested independently. In this lesson, treat “Business Logic and Use Cases” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Business Logic and Use Cases
content_blocks.expected_output: The request flow separates parsing, policy checks, use-case execution, and response serialization; dependency boundaries make each layer testable.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Keeping business rules outside controllers”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Reusable use-case functions” and “Maintaining domain invariants”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Keep controllers thin and make business rules testable without a live network request. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating business logic and use cases. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Keeping business rules outside controllers” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Business Logic and Use Cases with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating business logic and use cases as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: Separate request transport, application use cases, domain rules, and persistence so each responsibility can be tested independently. In this lesson, treat “Business Logic and Use Cases” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 102: Dependency Injection and Testability.
